# Thank you

We really appreciate your interest in contributing to this project. We welcome contributions of all kinds, including bug fixes, new features, documentation improvements, and more.

Please try to follow this and [The Project Conventions](CONVENTIONS.md) as closely as possible to keep the codebase consistent and maintainable. These are not hard rules, but it's best to follow them unless you have a good reason not to.

I won't go into the details of how to write Rust code or use Git here, but if you're new to either of those, there are plenty of great resources online to get you up to speed. This repository is not really suited for complete beginners, but if you're willing to learn and put in the effort, we welcome your contributions.


## Issues

Try to understand the following things before submitting an issue:

1. Is it a bug, a feature request, or a question? We have separate issue templates for each of these, so please use the appropriate one when creating an issue.

2. Is it already known? Please search the existing issues to see if your issue has already been reported or discussed. If it has, you can add any additional information or context you have to the existing issue instead of creating a new one. This also helps us avoid duplicates and keeps the issue tracker organized.
    2.1. If your issue was resolved, please consider closing it or marking it as resolved to help keep the issue tracker clean and up-to-date.

3. Provide as much detail as possible. This includes steps to reproduce the issue, expected vs actual behavior, screenshots or logs if applicable, and any other relevant information. The more details you provide, the easier it will be for us to understand and address the issue.

4. Be respectful and constructive. We are all volunteers working on this project in our free time, so please be patient and understanding if we don't respond immediately or if we need to ask for more information.


## Pull requests

You can submit a pull request for any issue, but it's best to discuss the issue first if it's a significant change or if you're not sure how to implement it. To do so, you follow pretty much the exact same steps for any open-source project:

1. Fork the repository and create a new branch for your changes.
2. Make your changes and commit them with clear and descriptive commit messages.
3. Push your branch to your forked repository.
4. Open a pull request against the **dev/** branch of the main repository, not **main/**. This helps us keep the main branch stable and production-ready while we continue development in the dev branch.
5. In the pull request description, explain what your changes do and reference any related issues.
6. Be responsive to any feedback or questions from the maintainers. We may request changes or ask for clarification, so please be open to discussion and willing to make adjustments as needed.

Make sure to follow the project's coding conventions and style guidelines when making your changes. This helps keep the codebase consistent and maintainable.


## AI contributions

While not strictly prohibited, we ask that you not use AI tools to generate code or documentation for this project, and using them will probably get your PR rejected. This is because of the complications around licensing and attribution, as well as general concerns about the quality and reliability of AI-generated content. If you do, however, use AI tools to assist you in writing code (*not documentation.*), please tell us which parts and which tools you used, so we can properly attribute the contribution and ensure that it complies with our requirements.


## Conventions and style conventions

These are documented in [CONVENTIONS.md](CONVENTIONS.md). Please try to follow these as closely as possible to keep the codebase consistent and maintainable. These are not hard rules, but it's best to follow them unless you have a good reason not to.
